professor.name: Dr. Gomez
professor.text: Many universities now record lectures and post them online. Some educators think this helps students learn because they can review difficult material at their own pace. Others worry that students stop attending class and lose the benefits of live discussion. What do you think? Should universities record all lectures and make them available online? Why or why not?

students.name: Kelly
students.text: I think recordings are very useful. When a professor speaks quickly, I can pause the video and take better notes. Students who are sick or who work part-time also don't fall behind.

students.name: Andrew
students.text: I disagree. If every lecture is online, many students will just stay home, and class discussions will become empty. Asking questions in person is an important part of learning.

professor.name: Professor Tan
professor.text: Cities around the world are trying to reduce traffic in their downtown areas. One approach is to make public transportation completely free. Supporters say this would encourage people to leave their cars at home. Critics argue that the money would be better spent improving service. If you were advising a city government, would you recommend free public transportation? Explain your view.

students.name: Maria
students.text: Free transportation is a great idea. Many people drive because bus tickets add up over a month. If buses were free, more people would try them, and there would be less pollution.

students.name: Jason
students.text: I'm not convinced. Price isn't the main problem where I live—the buses are slow and come only every half hour. A free bus that never arrives on time won't change anyone's habits.

professor.name: Dr. Williams
professor.text: Some companies have started offering employees a four-day work week with the same pay, as long as the work gets done. Supporters say workers become happier and more productive. Others believe it is unrealistic for many types of businesses. Do you think a four-day work week is a good idea for most companies? Why or why not?

students.name: Priya
students.text: I think it could work well. People who have more rest are more focused, so they might get the same amount done in four days. It would also help companies attract good workers.

students.name: Tom
students.text: It sounds nice, but it doesn't fit every job. Hospitals, stores, and restaurants need staff every day. Those businesses would have to hire more people, which could be very expensive.

professor.name: Professor Ahmed
professor.text: This week we are discussing how people form habits. Some researchers recommend changing one small habit at a time, while others suggest that big life changes, such as moving to a new city, are the best moment to change many habits at once. Which approach do you think is more effective for building good habits, and why?

students.name: Lucas
students.text: Small changes are more realistic. When I tried to change everything at once in January, I gave up after a week. Starting with one habit, like going to bed earlier, is easier to keep.

students.name: Hannah
students.text: I think big changes can actually help. When I moved to college, I had no old routine, so it was easy to start exercising and cooking. A new environment gives you a fresh start.

professor.name: Dr. Okafor
professor.text: Many supermarkets now charge customers a small fee for plastic bags. The goal is to reduce plastic waste, but some people say the fee is unfair to low-income shoppers or simply moves the problem elsewhere. In your opinion, is charging for plastic bags an effective way to protect the environment? Explain why.

students.name: Sofia
students.text: Yes, I think it works. In my town, people started bringing their own bags almost immediately after the fee was introduced. Even a small cost makes people think about their choices.

students.name: Daniel
students.text: I'm doubtful. Many people now buy plastic trash bags instead of reusing shopping bags, so the total amount of plastic may not change much. We need bigger solutions.

professor.name: Professor Hill
professor.text: Volunteering is often seen as an important part of being a good citizen. Some high schools now require students to complete a certain number of volunteer hours before they can graduate. Do you think schools should make volunteering a graduation requirement? Why or why not?

students.name: Emma
students.text: I support the requirement. Many teenagers never think about volunteering until someone asks them to. Once they try it, they often discover causes they care about.

students.name: Ryan
students.text: Forcing people to volunteer goes against the whole idea. Students will just do the minimum to get the hours, and organizations may end up with helpers who don't want to be there.

professor.name: Dr. Russo
professor.text: More and more people get their news from short videos on social media rather than from newspapers or television. Some say this makes news more accessible, especially for young people. Others worry that short videos cannot explain complex issues properly. What is your view? Is getting news from short videos a positive or negative trend?

students.name: Aiko
students.text: I see it as positive. Many of my friends never read newspapers, but they watch short news videos every day. At least they know what is happening in the world.

students.name: Marcus
students.text: The problem is that a one-minute video can't give context. People see a dramatic clip and form strong opinions without understanding the full story. That can make debates more extreme.

professor.name: Professor Lindqvist
professor.text: Governments sometimes provide financial support to industries they consider strategically important, such as renewable energy or computer chip manufacturing. Proponents argue that early support helps new industries become competitive. Critics contend that governments are poor at choosing winners and that subsidies distort markets. Should governments subsidize specific industries? Use reasons and examples to support your position.

students.name: Fatima
students.text: I think targeted support is justified when the benefits extend beyond a single company. Solar power became affordable partly because early subsidies allowed producers to scale up, and now the whole economy benefits from cheaper energy.

students.name: Oliver
students.text: Subsidies often end up protecting inefficient firms long after they should have adapted. Once an industry receives money, it lobbies to keep it. I'd prefer governments to fund basic research and let companies compete.

professor.name: Dr. Haddad
professor.text: Artificial intelligence tools can now write essays, summarize readings, and solve problems. Some instructors want to ban these tools in coursework, while others believe students should learn to use them responsibly as they will in the workplace. How do you think universities should respond to AI tools in student assignments? Explain your reasoning.

students.name: Grace
students.text: Banning them is unrealistic and probably impossible to enforce. Universities should redesign assignments so that students have to show their own reasoning, for example through drafts or oral explanations, while still allowing AI for brainstorming.

students.name: Victor
students.text: I think some courses should ban them, at least at the beginning. If students rely on AI before they've developed basic writing skills, they'll never learn to structure an argument themselves.

professor.name: Professor Lin
professor.text: Some cities have introduced taxes on sugary drinks to reduce health problems such as obesity and diabetes. Evidence suggests that consumption falls after such taxes are introduced, but critics say the taxes place a heavier burden on low-income families and limit personal choice. Do you think taxes on sugary drinks are a good public health policy? Why or why not?

students.name: Noah
students.text: The evidence is persuasive. If purchases drop and the revenue is spent on health programs or free drinking water in schools, low-income communities actually benefit the most.

students.name: Isabella
students.text: I'm uncomfortable with policies that change behavior by making daily life more expensive for people with the least money. Education and better access to healthy food would address the causes rather than punishing the symptoms.

professor.name: Dr. Moreau
professor.text: When historic buildings are no longer used for their original purpose, cities must decide what to do with them. Some argue that these buildings should be carefully preserved as they are, while others believe they should be adapted for new uses, even if this means significant changes to their interiors. Which approach do you favor, and why?

students.name: Elena
students.text: Adaptation keeps buildings alive. An old factory turned into apartments or a library is used every day, and the community stays connected to its history in a practical way.

students.name: James
students.text: Some changes destroy exactly what made a building valuable. Once original interiors are removed, they can't be restored. I think at least the most significant buildings should be protected from major alterations.

professor.name: Professor Diaz
professor.text: Many minority languages around the world are losing speakers as younger generations shift to more widely used languages. Some people believe that governments should invest heavily in preserving these languages through schools and media. Others argue that language change is natural and that resources should go elsewhere. What is your position on this issue?

students.name: Amara
students.text: A language carries knowledge, stories, and ways of seeing the world that can't be fully translated. When it disappears, that knowledge is lost for everyone, so public investment is worth it.

students.name: Ethan
students.text: Preservation programs often fail if families themselves don't see a benefit in using the language. Rather than large government programs, support should go to communities that actively want to keep their language.

professor.name: Dr. Carter
professor.text: Some companies publish the salaries of all their employees so that everyone can see what others earn. Supporters say this transparency reduces unfair pay gaps. Opponents worry that it creates conflict and invades employees' privacy. Should companies make all salaries public within the organization? Explain your view with reasons and examples.

students.name: Mei
students.text: Transparency forces companies to justify their decisions. Pay gaps between men and women, for example, are much harder to maintain when everyone can see the numbers.

students.name: Liam
students.text: Salaries depend on many factors that aren't visible, such as negotiation or special skills. Publishing them could lead to resentment and make employees feel judged by colleagues.

professor.name: Professor Brown
professor.text: Some schools give students a lot of homework every day. Other schools give very little homework so that students have time for sports, hobbies, and family. Which do you think is better for students: more homework or less homework? Why?

students.name: Mia
students.text: I think more homework is better. Practicing at home helps students remember what they learned in class, and it prepares them for exams.

students.name: Leo
students.text: I prefer less homework. Students are already tired after school. They need time to relax, play sports, and spend time with their families.

professor.name: Dr. Silva
professor.text: Many people use their phones right before they go to sleep. Some experts say this is bad for sleep, but others think it is a good way to relax. Should people stop using their phones one hour before bed? Why or why not?

students.name: Chloe
students.text: Yes, I think so. When I read on my phone at night, I fall asleep much later. Reading a paper book helps me sleep better.

students.name: Sam
students.text: I don't agree. Listening to music or watching a short video on my phone helps me relax after a busy day. It depends on what you do with the phone.

professor.name: Professor Kim
professor.text: Some people like to live in big cities, while others prefer small towns. Each place has advantages. If you could choose, would you prefer to live in a big city or a small town? Explain why.

students.name: Olivia
students.text: I would choose a big city. There are more jobs, museums, and restaurants, and public transportation makes it easy to go everywhere.

students.name: Ben
students.text: I prefer small towns. They are quieter and safer, and people know their neighbors. Life is less stressful when everything is close.

professor.name: Dr. Evans
professor.text: Many students have part-time jobs while they are studying at university. Some people think this is a good experience. Others think students should focus only on their studies. Is it a good idea for university students to have part-time jobs? Why or why not?

students.name: Zoe
students.text: Yes, it is a good idea. Students learn to manage money and time, and they get experience that helps them find a job after graduation.

students.name: Adam
students.text: I think students should focus on studying. A job takes a lot of time and energy, and grades can become worse.

professor.name: Professor Reyes
professor.text: Online shopping has become extremely popular, and many small local stores have closed as a result. Some people say this is simply progress and that customers benefit from lower prices and more choice. Others think communities lose something important when local shops disappear. What is your opinion? Should people make an effort to shop at local stores?

students.name: Nina
students.text: I try to shop locally when I can. Local stores create jobs in the neighborhood and make streets more lively. Saving a few dollars online isn't worth losing that.

students.name: Chris
students.text: Most people simply can't afford to pay more. Online shopping saves time and money, especially for busy families. Stores need to adapt instead of expecting customers to support them.

professor.name: Dr. Park
professor.text: Some universities require all first-year students to take courses outside their major, such as art, history, or science. Supporters say this gives students a broader education. Others think students should be free to focus on their chosen field from the start. Should universities require students to take courses outside their major? Why or why not?

students.name: Rachel
students.text: Yes. I took a philosophy course I didn't want to take, and it completely changed the way I think about my engineering projects. You can't know what's useful until you try it.

students.name: Kevin
students.text: University is expensive, and students should be able to spend their time and money on what they actually need for their careers. Required courses can feel like a waste.
